title: Julian of Norwich (c. 1343–after 1416)
hookLine: a woman walled in beside a church sees that all shall be well

lines: A ROOM AGAINST A CHURCH WALL.
ONE WINDOW IN, ONE WINDOW OUT.
cards: Against the wall of a church in Norwich, in England, stands a small room. One window looks into the church, toward the altar, so the woman inside can follow the Mass.
Another opens to the outside, so people from the town can come and talk to her. She doesn't come out. She chose this, with the Church's blessing, and she will spend her life here, praying.
Her own name isn't certain. History knows her by the name of the church, Saint Julian's.

teach.h: ENCLOSED BESIDE A CHURCH, FOR LIFE.
teach.b: Start with the word. An anchoress is a woman who, with the bishop's blessing, is enclosed for life in a cell attached to a church, to give her days to prayer. A man who did the same was called an anchorite.
It sounds like a prison, but it was a vocation, asked for and tested, and people from the town could come to the window for counsel. Next, the showings.
Julian writes that she once fell so sick that those around her thought she was dying. A priest held a crucifix before her eyes.

Then, she says, she was given a series of showings, visions of Christ's passion and of God's love, and she spent years thinking about them and writing them down. The book is called Revelations of Divine Love.

teach.h: A PROMISE FROM INSIDE THE PAIN.
teach.b: Julian lived in the same century as yesterday's plague, and she doesn't look away from sin or pain. She asks, plainly, why God allowed sin at all.
The answer she hears, in Grace Warrack's translation, is this: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." Finally, what the line is not.
It isn't a shrug, and it isn't a promise that nothing bad will happen. Julian hears it in the middle of her question about sin and suffering, and she keeps asking afterward.
It's a promise spoken from inside the pain, about where things are going, not a denial of where they are.

how: Catholics read Julian's Revelations of Divine Love in prayer groups and on retreat, and some visit her rebuilt cell at Saint Julian's Church in Norwich; she is honored as Blessed or as a saint in different calendars, though she has not been formally canonized.

Julian heard all shall be well while asking why God allowed sin
the promise comes in the middle of her hardest question, not instead of it.

games.q: you're Julian, shown God's love, and still troubled. sin and pain are everywhere. what do you do with your question?
o: drop it; it's not your place to ask.
ask it plainly, and keep asking.
decide the showings must have been a dream.
games.why: she asks why God allowed sin at all, and hears: all shall be well. and she keeps thinking and writing for years afterward.

practice: Let one real worry come to mind, not the biggest, and look at it honestly without pretending it's fine.
Then, on each slow out-breath, say Julian's words quietly: all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well.
If you pray, let them be your prayer; if not, notice what it's like to hold a worry and a hope at once.

wordCard.voice: Anchoress. A woman enclosed for life in a cell beside a church, given to prayer, with one window toward the altar and one toward the town. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: all shall be well. Julian kept asking, and she kept hoping too. Until tomorrow.
